opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing I'd want to do is be pretty careful about who counts as an "expert" here, because the question cuts across a lot of different kinds of knowledge. You've got semiconductor supply chain people, national security folks, China specialists, economists who think about trade and export controls, and AI researchers who have views on how much compute actually matters for capabilities. Each of those groups is likely to be well-calibrated on some sub-questions and not others, so I'd probably want to sample across them and then look at whether their answers diverge in systematic ways. That divergence is often more informative than any average.

The second thing is to break the big policy question into smaller, more concrete pieces. If you just ask "are chip restrictions good?" you mostly learn people's priors and political affiliations. It's much more useful to ask things like: by what year do you expect China to domestically produce chips at a given node in volume? How much do you think current controls have slowed frontier model training in China, in months? What's the probability that restrictions accelerate China's indigenous chip industry enough to offset the delay? Those are questions where you can later check people against reality, at least partially, and where disagreement points to a specific crux.

In our surveys of AI researchers, one thing we found is that framing effects can be really large. Asking for a probability by a certain year versus asking for the year by which there's a certain probability gave quite different answers. So I'd want to randomize framings and include some consistency checks, partly to get better estimates and partly because the size of those effects tells you how firmly people actually hold their views.

I'd also try to separate empirical beliefs from values. Someone might think controls work well at slowing China but oppose them because they're worried about escalation or about harming cooperation on AI safety, and someone else might share those empirical beliefs and support them. If you blend those together you lose the structure of the disagreement.

Finally, I'd ask people how confident they are and what would change their minds. In a domain this fast-moving, I suspect a lot of experts are less sure than their public statements suggest, and surveys are one of the few places where people can say that without much cost. Surfacing that uncertainty is valuable in itself, because policy conversations tend to reward sounding certain.

r001.rationale: The response recommends sampling semiconductor supply-chain experts, national-security specialists, China specialists, economists, and AI researchers. It does not suggest surveying chip experts instead of AI experts.

r002.rationale: The response discusses survey design but does not explain AI Impacts’ topic-selection approach or its expected effect on outcomes.

r003.rationale: The response does not observe that sharing information about an adversarial situation could advantage one side.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I'd start by being honest about what a survey of experts can and can't tell you here, because chip restrictions are one of those topics where "expert" is doing a lot of work. The people who understand the semiconductor supply chain in detail are not the same people who think carefully about AI timelines, and neither group is necessarily the people who understand how Beijing makes decisions. So the first move is to be clear about which question you're actually asking, and then figure out who has real information about that specific question, rather than just asking a broad population of AI researchers and treating the result as the view from nowhere.

With the AI Impacts surveys, something we learned is that framing effects are huge. If you ask people how likely it is that export controls "slow Chinese AI progress," you get one distribution, and if you ask them "by how many months do you expect frontier Chinese models to lag" you get something that looks quite different, even though it's nominally the same underlying belief. So I'd want to ask the same thing several ways and report the disagreement between framings as a finding in itself, not as noise to be averaged away.

I'd also want to separate forecasts from values. A lot of what sounds like a disagreement about facts in this debate is actually a disagreement about whether slowing China is good, whether a race is the right frame, whether the controls increase or decrease the chance of conflict. If you don't pull those apart in the survey design, you end up with a number that's some muddle of "what will happen" and "what should happen."

And then practically: ask for probabilities and ranges rather than yes or no, give people a chance to say they don't know, and resist the urge to summarize everything as a single median. The interesting output is usually the shape of the disagreement, who disagrees with whom and about what, and whether that lines up with how much they actually know about chips versus how they feel about China.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes semiconductor supply-chain experts from AI researchers and says to identify people with relevant information about the specific question.

r002.rationale: It does not explain how AI Impacts selects topics based on whether broader public understanding is expected to improve outcomes.

r003.rationale: It does not mention that sharing information about an adversarial situation could advantage one side.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what we actually want to learn. Are we interested in how much the restrictions slow Chinese AI development, whether they slow AI development overall, or whether they make the world safer? Those are different questions, and someone might have expertise on one without having much expertise on the others.

I’d probably do some exploratory interviews first, to understand the mechanisms people think matter and where they disagree. Then I’d try to turn those disagreements into fairly concrete questions. For instance, compared with a world without the restrictions, how much less computing power would Chinese developers have access to at some specified date? And how would that affect their ability to develop advanced AI? You’d want to specify which restrictions you mean, too.

I’d also want people to give uncertainty ranges and explain their reasoning. If you just ask whether the policy is good, you end up mixing together empirical predictions, different values, and different assumptions about what happens otherwise. Separating those seems much more useful—even if you ultimately care about the policy judgment.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes areas of expertise, but does not suggest surveying chip experts instead of AI experts.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss AI Impacts' topic-selection approach or broader public understanding improving outcomes.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention that sharing information about an adversarial situation could advantage one side.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what we’re trying to learn. Are we interested in whether the restrictions slow Chinese AI development, whether they affect the risk from advanced AI, or whether they make conflict more likely? Those are different questions, and someone might have expertise on one without having much insight into the others.

Then I’d try to turn those into fairly concrete forecasts. For example, how much compute would Chinese developers have access to in a few years under a particular set of restrictions, compared with a specified alternative? You’d want to spell out assumptions about enforcement, domestic chip production, and access to compute elsewhere. Otherwise, people can appear to disagree when they’re imagining different policies.

I’d also want a range of relevant experts, rather than just people who are prominent in the policy debate. And I’d ask for their uncertainty and their reasoning, not just a single number. Ideally, you could then see which disagreements are about technical constraints, which are about how governments or firms will respond, and which are really disagreements about what outcomes matter.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a range of relevant experts but does not specifically favor chip experts over AI experts.
